The exact change of ST-SUP-RP14-LC05 is in the design input ST-SUP-RP14-LC05.change.json of the builder b-wt4fix.

title: Must a write of a command or a worker stage the same change event as a collection write?
description: Found by the fifth walkthrough (G9), 2026-11-17. A collection write through the REST API stages one change event in its transaction (ST-SUP-RC20-OC40), so a Kafka consumer sees each create, update and delete. A write through the command handle, in a command (ST-SUP-RC32) or a worker (ST-SUP-RC35), stages none: a consumer does not see the orders that a command placed or the stock that a worker moved, and a read model that a consumer keeps from the change events goes stale with no sign. Options: (a) each write through the handle stages the same change event as a collection write of the same row, in the same transaction; (b) a command or a worker sends only the domain events that it declares as effects, and no change event; (c) both: (a) for each write, and the declared effects stay the domain events of the command or the worker. Recommendation: (c). The change event is a fact of the entity, not of the path that wrote the row: Rails update_all and Django QuerySet.update skip callbacks and signals and are known causes of stale caches and search indexes, and change data capture (Debezium) sees each committed row change whatever the writer. A domain event tells why the rows changed, which a change event cannot tell, so it stays explicit, as the outbox pattern does it. The outbox gives the order: each event is staged in the transaction of its write, so it is sent only after the commit, never after a rollback or a replay, and the events of one row keep the order of their commits with the same message key. Decision: (c), decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17. ST-SUP-RP10-LC36 states the change event of the handle, ST-SUP-RC32-OC14 and ST-SUP-RC35-OC14 make the generators give the event names, and ST-SUP-RC20-OC40 names the handle.

title: Which settings may a need name hold?
description: Found by the security review of PR #331 (F1, low), 2026-11-14. A need name such as '{service}-{settings.<key>}' may hold the value of any setting of its component that is not marked secret (ST-SUP-EN09, field Platform needs; ST-SUP-INV23). A setting that holds a password but is not marked, a namespace, an issuer or a URL then goes into platform-requirements.yaml, which ST-DLV-INV02 forbids, and into Kubernetes object names, which events, audit logs and each reader of the namespace see. A variable name already takes only a setting whose enum holds names alone (ST-SUP-EN14, field Name). Options: (a) a component marks each setting that may go into a name; (b) refuse settings of a secret, namespace, URL or issuer kind; (c) take only a text setting that is not secret and whose schema allows only a closed list of values (an enum) that each fit the name. Recommendation: (c). (a) and (b) trust a mark or a list of kinds that an author can forget, as a secret that is not marked shows; an enum is fixed when the component is reviewed, so no value of an environment or of a free text can reach a name, and it is the rule that variable names already use. No shipped component uses a setting in a need name now, so nothing breaks. Decision: (c), decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17.

title: How does a command of a gRPC service create a row with no parent, and what does checking do with a collection of a service that has no rest-api?
description: Found by the sixth walkthrough (N3, K4), 2026-11-17. A command must name a resource member (ST-DECL-INV40), and the command generator needs an entity with the resource type of the command, whose row token Run reads FOR SHARE (ST-SUP-RP10-LC31). So in a service with no rest-api, such as notifier (rpc-service), no command can write the first Notice: no row exists that the permission can be decided on. Run already decides a create of an entity with no parent on the service-level resource of the tenant provisioning, by its tenant-qualified ID (ST-SUP-RP10-LC31, ST-SUP-Q127), and a CRUD create uses it (ST-SUP-RC29-OC01), but a declared command cannot ask for it. Also, a collection in an rpc-service passes checking, and no component serves it (K4). Options for the create: (a) a command whose resource type is the resource type of the tenant provisioning names no resource member, and Run decides its permission on the tenant-qualified service-level resource, as a CRUD create of an entity with no parent; such a command only creates rows with no parent; (b) a command may be public, with no resource; (c) generate the standard gRPC methods of AIP-131 to AIP-135 from each collection. Options for the collection: (d) checking refuses a collection that no active component serves; (e) the grpc-application component serves collections. Recommendation: (a) and (d). AIP-133 gives a top-level Create no parent field, and Google Cloud, GitHub and SpiceDB decide a create on the container (organization, account or a platform object), never on the new row; STEGO already does this for a CRUD create, so (a) adds no new path and no bypass. (b) breaks fail-closed authorization (ST-DECL-INV31). (c) and (e) are a second CRUD surface with its own proto generation: a later feature, if a user needs it. A declaration that the generator accepts and then does not serve is a known source of defects (Kubernetes added strict field validation for this), so (d) refuses the collection and tells the author to use commands and queries. Decision: the recommendation, decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17. ST-DECL-INV40 lets such a command name no resource member, ST-SUP-RC32-OC15 states how it is generated and run, and ST-DECL-INV92 refuses a collection that no active component serves.

title: Does a grant on a scoped resource reach the rows below it through the scoped routes, when the caller may not read an ancestor above it?
description: Found by the sixth walkthrough (K9), 2026-11-17. A project of a workspace was shared with bob as viewer. Every CRUD route of the project, its tickets and its comments answered 404 to bob, because the chain check decides the read permission on each ancestor of the path (ST-SUP-RC20-OC24, ST-SUP-Q129 (A)), and bob may not view the workspace. The query ticket-card and the list open-tickets gave bob the same tickets. So one row has two policies, one for the path and one for the query. Options: (a) keep the read decision on each ancestor; (b) decide only on the deepest resource that the request names, check each ancestor above it for existence and for its link to the next one only, and state any rule that an ancestor permission must also hold in the authorization schema, such as permission view = viewer & parent->view; (c) a separate traverse permission on each ancestor, which a share must also write. Recommendation: (b). Zanzibar and SpiceDB keep the policy in the schema, and a permission of a row already includes its parents by an arrow (parent->view); GitHub lets an outside collaborator use org/repo without a view of the organization; Google Drive opens a shared file in a folder that the user cannot open; Confluence shows that the opposite rule, a restricted parent that hides each child, is an intersection that a schema can state. (c) is the POSIX execute bit, which Windows turns off for Everyone by default (Bypass traverse checking), and it needs a second tuple per share that must be revoked with it. (a) cannot state a share below the top level at all. The security of (b): a caller without a grant on the deepest resource gets the same 404, with the same calls, for a missing, wrong or denied path; the stored row is still checked against the parent of the path, so a path cannot reach a row of another parent (OWASP API1:2023); a caller with a grant on the deepest resource learns no field of an ancestor; it can learn, from 200 against 404, whether an ancestor above the parent is linked to the next one, and the href of the row names each ancestor, so at two or more levels it learns more than the parent ID that the row holds (security review of PR #409, L4); a caller with no grant on it learns nothing of the ancestors. Decision: the recommendation, decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17. ST-SUP-RC20-OC24 states the new check; ST-SUP-Q129 stays as history.

title: How does the database of a browser-service get its schema, and what does a refused start name?
description: Found by the sixth walkthrough (K10, N6), 2026-11-17. The browser-service binary has no migrate mode. The README of browser-backend tells the author to call browser/schema.Bootstrap from Go code of their own (ST-SUP-RC02-OC49). With the session table made by hand, the binary stopped with only stage database.access and no cause (ST-SUP-RC02-OC50, OC52). A rest-crud service runs one migration job in the mode migrate (ST-SUP-RP14-LC03), which the Kubernetes base writes (ST-DLV-INV13), and a refused start names its stage (ST-SUP-RP14-LC05). Options: (a) keep the hand bootstrap and document it; (b) the minimum: the browser-service binary accepts the mode migrate, which runs Bootstrap as the owner and Verify as the runtime login, the Kubernetes base writes the same migration Job, and a refused Verify names its fault class; (c) move the session table onto the migration ledger and the schema manifest of the service runtime now. Recommendation: (b) now, and (c) when browser-service joins the runtime data path (single data path, 2026-11-11). Flyway, Liquibase and Rails all run the migration as one separate step with its own privileged credential, and the Kubernetes Job before the rollout is the usual form; a schema that each user writes by hand is the failure that these tools were made to stop, and an error with no cause makes each operator read the code. The security of (b): the owner credential stays in the Job only (ST-SUP-RP04-LC06, ST-DLV-INV13), and the fault class names a fixed object kind of the generated schema, never a value, a secret or a role password. Decision: the recommendation, decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17. ST-SUP-RC02-OC56 adds the mode and the Job, and ST-SUP-RC02-OC57 names the fault.

title: Does STEGO offer a component that consumes the Kafka events of another service, and what is its minimum design?
description: Found by the sixth walkthrough (N1), 2026-11-17. The change events of tracker reached its topic (ST-SUP-RP01-LC30), and no component lets notifier consume them; a consuming worker takes only a destination of its own outbox (ST-SUP-RC35-OC06). Options: (a) no component, and each author writes a consumer; (b) a kafka-consumer component that writes each record into the inbox and gives it to a consuming worker; (c) Kafka exactly-once transactions. Recommendation: (b), as an alpha component. Kafka exactly-once covers only a read, process and write inside Kafka, not a database write, so (c) does not apply. The inbox and idempotent consumer patterns (microservices.io, NServiceBus, MassTransit) are the known answer: the consumer stores the message ID in the same transaction as its effect, so a redelivery after a rebalance or a crash is a no-op. The minimum: a declared subscription names the source service, the topic need and the event kinds; in the worker mode the component reads the topic in the consumer group <service>.<subscription>, with enable.auto.commit off; for each record it checks the headers that ST-SUP-RP01-LC30 sends (event ID, kind, stego-tenant), the kind against the declared list, the tenant against the tenant list, and the size, and inserts it into the service outbox as a message of the consumed destination of the worker, with the unique key (subscription, event ID) and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; it commits the offset only after that transaction commits. Then the consuming worker runs it as today, with its idempotency key, its order per key, its retries and its parking. A record that fails a check is stored parked with an alert and a fixed reason, never skipped in silence and never left to block its partition (the poison pill of Kafka consumers; Uber and Kafka Connect use a dead letter queue for this). The dedup rows stay at least as long as the topic retention. Trust: the payload holds only the entity, the action and the row ID (ST-SUP-Q114), the stego-tenant header is trusted only because the platform lets only the source service write the topic (an ACL need that env check reads), and the consumer uses the TLS and SASL settings of ST-SUP-RP01-LC32. Decision: the recommendation, decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17. The builder adds the component kafka-consumer with its output contracts, the declaration entity of a subscription and its invariants (technical stage after this decision), after the rank 1 gaps of the sixth walkthrough. Detail decided with the builder, 2026-11-17: a record of a kind of the source service that the subscription does not declare is skipped and counted, not refused, because the topic of an entity carries every action; a kind of another service is refused. A refused record is kept in the table stego_inbox.refused with its fixed reason for 30 days, purged on the timer of the outbox, and never holds a header text that failed its check, because a record of an unknown tenant has no tenant that can own an outbox row. While the component is alpha a service has one subscription, because its topic and group settings have fixed names. The ID of an inbox message is a UUID version 5 over the subscription, the tenant and the event ID; the inbox does not start when the topic keeps its records longer than the outbox keeps a done message, or without end with no setting that accepts it, because an offset reset to an older record can apply it twice. The staging principal of an inbox message is the service account of the consuming worker, and the subscription is its stager.

title: What must a refused consuming worker report, how are outbox destinations kept apart, and how does a worker list read its rows?
description: Found by the sixth walkthrough (K5, K6, K8), 2026-11-17. (a) K5: the message of notify-assignee stayed pending with delivery-refused for 12 attempts and more, with no log line and no worker.run.failed. A fill error is a transient refusal (ST-SUP-RC35-OC06), and a must-land message is never parked for a retry (ST-SUP-RP01-LC23), so a fill that fails the same way each time runs for ever. Only not_granted is reported. (b) K6: while Kafka refused each event, the authz relay and the audit sink waited 30 to 80 s, because one pool of four slots serves every destination (ST-SUP-RP01-LC05). (c) K8: a worker fill gives its own SQL in command.ListSpec, with the column list of its Scan, so an added column breaks it, and the failed run names no cause. Options and recommendations: (a) each failed attempt of a consuming worker MUST emit worker.run.failed with the outcome and a fixed cause class and one warn log line with the worker, the destination, the event ID and the attempt, as the Kafka destination logs topic-refused (ST-SUP-RP01-LC31-T06), and a fill error or panic that repeats 5 times MUST park the message as poison with the alert of ST-SUP-RP01-LC12; an undecided provider stays transient. Spring Kafka gives up after 10 failures, RabbitMQ 4.0 added a default delivery limit of 20 against poison messages, and SQS and Azure Service Bus use a max receive count; a parked message stays in the outbox and can be sent again, so must land still holds. (b) each registered destination MUST get its own claim and its own slots, a bulkhead (Azure Architecture Center, Resilience4j, Hystrix), so a slow or refused destination uses only its own slots and the authz relay always has a slot. (c) workers MUST read through a declared list that the generator emits from the entity, with the same predicates as queries, and a fill MUST NOT give SQL: a hand column list breaks at each expand step (parallel change), and SQL text from a fill is a path to storage that ST-SUP-RP10-LC02 forbids for the handle. Decision: the recommendation, decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17. ST-SUP-RC35-OC06 gets the report and the poison bound, ST-SUP-RP01-LC34 states the bulkhead, ST-DECL-INV94 and ST-SUP-RC35-OC15 state the declared list, and ST-SUP-RP10-LC38 makes NewList take only a generated list.

title: How does a tenant administrator grant a further person a relation on the service-level resource of the tenant?
description: Found by core builder 13 with walkthrough-7 NB2, 2026-11-17. Provision now gives the first administrators of a new tenant the declared admin relation on the tenant-qualified service-level resource (ST-SUP-RC27-OC13). After that, no STEGO path writes a further grant on that resource: relationships_written takes only a relation of the SpiceDB type of an entity that the command writes, and the service-level resource is not an entity; so only the operator, with a direct write to SpiceDB (zed), can make a second dispatcher. Options: (a) a command on the service-level resource (ST-SUP-RC32-OC15) may name relationships_written: [<resource type>#<relation>], and its helpers relate and unrelate a person on the tenant-qualified service-level resource of the request tenant only, decided by the command's own permission, with the relations tenant, worker_<name> and every relation that the provision or the retire permission reaches refused by checking; (b) a fixed runtime endpoint POST <base path>/stego/grants, decided on a declared grant permission; (c) keep the operator's direct write, and document it. Prior art: GitHub, Google Cloud and SpiceDB let an owner of the container add a member through the same API as any other change, decided by a manage permission on the container. Recommendation: (a), because it adds no new endpoint kind, reuses the decision, audit, outbox and relay of a command, and keeps every grant in one tenant (ST-SUP-RP06-LC22). Until it is decided, the docs give the zed command and the two ID forms.

title: How does the base leave out a variable that the generated service never reads?
description: Found by walkthrough 7 (B6), 2026-11-17. The Deployment of the browser-service portal wires STEGO_WORKER_DATABASE_URL (Secret portal-database, key worker-url), STEGO_RELAY_DATABASE_URL_FILE and STEGO_QUERY_CURSOR_KEY_FILE. Only the runtime library reads them (the command and outbox packages, and the query package), and the portal imports no runtime package, so the operator must make Secrets that nothing reads, and env check asks for them. Each component lists its variables whatever the declaration holds; only read_by_mode (migrate) leaves a variable out of the Deployment. Options: (a) ST-SUP-EN14 gets the field Read with: the runtime package that reads the variable, such as command, outbox or query; the platform requirements, the reference and the base list the variable only when the generated service imports that package, which the compiler already knows (it pins the runtime only when generated code imports it); (b) the variable states the declaration parts that make it read (commands, queries, workers, change events), and the requirements list it only when the declaration holds one; (c) leave it, and document that a browser-service needs the Secrets. Recommendation: (a). It follows the code that reads the value, as Score (a workload asks only for the resources it uses) and Helm charts that gate env entries on the feature that reads them; it needs no second copy of the rules that decide which runtime package a declaration uses, which (b) does and which drifts. (c) keeps a false need in env check, the failure the walkthrough found. Decision: (a), decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17: each environment entry of a component names the runtime package that reads it (field Read with), and requirements and the base list a variable only when the generated service imports that package (least privilege, derived from the code, not hand-listed).

title: How does a browser service reach more than one API without an open proxy?
description: Found by the eighth walkthrough (W8-N2), 2026-11-17. browser-backend has one api_prefix and one STEGO_BROWSER_API_URL (ST-SUP-RC02-OC07: one API origin), so the portal could not reach fulfilment (/api/fulfilment/v1 gave 404). Prior art: nginx gives each location its own fixed proxy_pass, and proxy_pass to a variable from the request (such as $arg_host or $http_host) is the classic open proxy and SSRF; the off-by-slash alias of a location reads files out of its root (Orange Tsai, Breaking Parser Logic, 2018). Next.js rewrites map a source path to a fixed destination, and CVE-2024-34351 was an SSRF through a Host header that chose the upstream. Envoy routes match a path prefix to one fixed cluster and normalize the path (merge_slashes, normalize_path) before the match. The Spring Cloud Gateway route list maps Path predicates to a fixed uri; CVE-2022-22947 let a caller add a route at run time through the actuator. The OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications draft (IETF OAuth WG, the BFF pattern) keeps the tokens in the backend and sends them only to known resource servers. Options: (a) keep one API and tell authors to put an API gateway behind it; (b) a declared list of APIs, each with a fixed prefix and a fixed upstream that the process environment gives at start; (c) an upstream that the request names, in a header or a path part. (c) is an open proxy and is refused. Recommendation: (b). The setting apis of browser-backend lists 1 to 8 entries {name, prefix} beside api_prefix, which stays the first API with STEGO_BROWSER_API_URL; name is lower case with hyphens, at most 32 characters, and unique; each prefix follows the rules of api_prefix, is unique, and is not a path-segment prefix of another prefix or of a reserved route. The URL of each named API comes from the one setting STEGO_BROWSER_API_URLS, a comma-separated list of name=https-origin, read once at start: start refuses a missing, unknown or repeated name, and an address that ST-SUP-RC02-OC36 refuses; all APIs share STEGO_BROWSER_API_CA_FILE. The proxy refuses a path with an encoded slash, a dot segment or an empty segment before it matches, then takes the entry whose prefix is the longest whole-segment match, and sends the request to that entry's origin only, with the allow list of ST-SUP-RC02-OC07; no header, query or path part of the request chooses a host, a port or a scheme, and the table never changes after start. Each API has its own bounded client, so a slow API does not take the capacity of another. A Location of an answer must sit under the prefix of the same entry. The same server-held access token goes to each API, so the token of the identity provider must hold the audience of each API in aud, and each API checks its own audience; a token of its own for each API (token exchange, RFC 8693) is out of scope now. Decision: the recommendation, decided by the orchestrator under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-17.

title: How does a gRPC client read its own write at once?
description: Found by walkthrough 9 (W9-B1), 2026-11-18. Over HTTP a write answers Authz-Revocation: pending and Authz-Revocation-Location (ST-SUP-RP10-LC35), and a read or query with Authz-Revocation-After waits for that revocation (ST-SUP-RP11-LC21, ST-SUP-RC20-OC41, ST-SUP-RC20-OC42, ST-SUP-RC33-OC10). Over gRPC no record states an equivalent: the command's ServeRPC answers no revocation metadata, so a gRPC client never learns the identity of its revocation, and query.ServeRPC and ServeStream read no such metadata. Thus a gRPC client that reads right after its write can get NotFound until the relay delivers the tuples. Prior art: gRPC metadata is the place for data of a call that is not part of the method's messages (the gRPC metadata guide), as the idempotency key already is (ST-SUP-RC07-OC19, metadata idempotency-key); SpiceDB itself returns its ZedToken in a message field, but that is its own API, and a field in each declared message couples the domain messages to the runtime. Options: (a) metadata: the gRPC answer of a command that enqueued a tuple sends the header metadata authz-revocation: pending and authz-revocation-location with the path of the status route; a unary query or stream reads the request metadata authz-revocation-after (the identity or the path, one value only) and waits through AwaitWrite at most the wait cap, the request metadata prefer (wait=N) and the deadline of the call, and sends authz-revocation with the last state in the header metadata; a bad value is InvalidArgument; this changes the command and query runtime (ServeRPC, ServeStream) and the grpc-application guide; (b) no gRPC form: a gRPC client that must read its own write reads through the HTTP route, and the guide says so; (c) a field in the declared messages: refused, it couples each message to the runtime. Recommendation: (a). It gives both transports the same rule with the same bounds, keeps the declared messages free of runtime fields, and follows the idempotency key, which already travels as metadata. It needs a runtime change (builder of registry/runtime) and output contracts on the command, query and grpc-application components. Decision: (a). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: the gRPC metadata keys authz-revocation, authz-revocation-location, authz-revocation-after and prefer carry read after write, with the call deadline as an extra bound.

title: How does a worker create a row with no parent, such as the local copy of an event of another service?
description: Found by the tenth walkthrough (B2), 2026-11-18. A worker that writes only root entities, each with a resource type and no set reference to an entity with a resource type, passes every check, and each run then fails: the worker handle decides a create on the parent resource that the call names and refuses a create with none (ST-SUP-RP10-LC17), and the log names only fill_error. A consumer that keeps a local copy of the events of another service (event-carried state transfer) needs such a create, and it is the first use of a subscription (ST-SUP-RC35-OC16). Today the author must first make a parent row through a command, only to have something to decide on. Options: (a) checking refuses a worker that writes an entity with a resource type that no create of the worker can decide on; this also refuses a worker that only updates or deletes such rows, and leaves the local copy with no way to start. (b) A worker's create of an entity with a resource type and no set reference is decided on the tenant resource of the run, tenant:<tenant-qualified ID> (authz.TenantResource, ST-SUP-Q132), which already holds the worker's own tuple tenant#worker_<name>@service_account:<name> (ST-SUP-RC35-OC13): the worker's declared permission with its service account as subject, and in RunConsumer a second time with the staging principal and the stager's permission, as ST-SUP-RP10-LC17 states for each other resource; generation refuses a worker that writes such an entity when the type tenant of the schema has no permission with the worker's permission name, and names the worker, the entity and the permission, so the author adds, for example, permission track = worker_track_patients to the type tenant. (c) As (b), but on the service-level resource of the tenant provisioning, as for a command create with no parent (ST-SUP-RC32-OC15). Recommendation: (b). Prior art: Zanzibar and SpiceDB decide the create of a top-level object on its container, such as an organization, never on the new row; Kubernetes decides a create on its namespace; AIP-133 gives a top-level Create no parent and IAM decides it on the project. The tenant resource is the container of each row of a tenant, already holds the worker's tuple, and is tenant-qualified, so the grant allows the create in one tenant only and no new tuple or relation path is needed. (c) needs a path from the service-level resource to the tenant's worker tuple, which no record gives. (a) blocks the use case. Until the decision, checking warns for each worker and each such entity that it writes (ST-SUP-RP10-LC17-T03; builder 20 under the owner's delegation, 2026-11-18), and the runtime builder makes the log of the refusal name its cause. Decision: (b). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: a worker's create of a row with no parent is decided on the tenant resource with the worker's declared permission (ST-SUP-RP10-LC17), and generation refuses a schema whose tenant type lacks that permission (ST-SUP-RC35-OC17).

title: How does a command on the service-level resource read rows to check a rule, such as a free slot?
description: Found by the tenth walkthrough (B3, step 06), 2026-11-18. A command whose resource type is the resource type of the tenant provisioning is decided on the service-level resource, and its handle offers only the create and the read by ID of each entity that it writes (ST-SUP-RC32-OC15), so the generator refuses each list that it declares. Thus a create such as book-appointment cannot check a rule against other rows, such as the slot is free or a patient has at most three bookings in a day. Also a list may read only an entity that the command writes (ST-DECL-INV94), so to read PatientCard the command must write it, and the handle then offers a create of PatientCard that the command does not need. Options: (a) a command on the service-level resource may declare read-only lists, with no lock: the handle offers List and not ListForUpdate, each row is decided with the list permission of the entity for the caller, as the list of a query (ST-SUP-RP11-LC07), and a denied row is dropped; a new field reads names an entity that the command lists and never writes, so the handle offers no create of it. The read is not locked, so a rule that must hold under two calls at once still needs a key in the database. (b) As (a), and also locked lists (lock: true), decided on the list permission of the entity: two calls at once see each other's rows, but a caller then holds a row lock FOR UPDATE on rows that it may only read, which can block the writers of those rows up to the run bound. (c) No list: a rule over rows is a unique key (unique: true, or a composite unique key) or a database constraint, and the conflict of SQLSTATE 23505 answers a declared refusal that names the key, such as appointment.slot_taken, in place of the code conflict. (d) No change: model the set as a parent aggregate, such as a Calendar, and give the command its resource member; a command on the parent locks it with GetForUpdate and lists its children with the parent term, which ST-DECL-INV94 and ST-SUP-RP10-LC05 already allow. Recommendation: (a) with (c). Prior art: in domain-driven design, a rule over a set of aggregates (set validation, such as a unique user name or a free slot) is held by a unique index or an exclusion constraint in the database, or by an aggregate that owns the set; a read in the command is a check for a better message, not the guard. PostgreSQL gives EXCLUDE USING gist for overlapping time slots, and booking systems use it for this reason. Google AIP-132 decides a List on its parent; the list of a STEGO query decides each row for the caller (ST-SUP-RP11-LC07), which is stricter and fits a list in a command. (a) reuses the decision of a query list and adds no lock that the command's permission does not cover; (c) makes the race-free rule declarable and its answer specific; (b) adds a lock that a reader can hold on rows that it may not change; (d) works today, but forces a parent aggregate on each rule. Not built; the walkthrough uses unique: true on slot, which answers 409 conflict.

title: Must the migration ledger hold a hash of the body of each step, so a changed body of an applied step is refused?
description: Found by the security review of PR #417 (L2), 2026-11-17. The ledger stego_schema.migrations records the name of each applied migration, and CheckLedger compares names only (ST-SUP-RC01-OC41). Thus a release that changes the body of a step that a database already applied never brings that change to that database, and nothing tells the operator. This occurred: postgres-adapter 6.10 added the within CHECK by a change of the body of the existing step migration and of 001_initial, so a database that applied that step under 6.8 or 6.9 never gets the CHECK. Prior art: Flyway records a CRC32 checksum of each versioned migration in flyway_schema_history, and validate (on by default before migrate) stops with a checksum mismatch; repair writes the new checksums. Liquibase records an MD5 checksum of each changeset in DATABASECHANGELOG and stops update on a mismatch, unless the changeset sets runOnChange or validCheckSum. Atlas writes atlas.sum, a hash of each file and of the whole migration folder, and refuses to lint or apply a folder whose files do not agree with it. golang-migrate and the Rails schema_migrations table record only the version (golang-migrate adds a dirty flag after a failed step), so an edited applied step is never run and never reported. Known failures: Flyway and Liquibase gave false mismatches for a change of line endings, of the file encoding or of the checksum version (Liquibase 4.22 changed to checksum version 9 and normalized the text), and teams then ran repair or clear-checksums as routine, which removed the protection; a checksum with no rule for the fix tells the operator only that something changed. Options: (a) keep names only, and state that the body of a released step never changes: a fix is a new step; (b) a hash in the ledger: each row records the SHA-256 of the exact body of its step, and CheckLedger refuses a database whose applied step has another hash, with a fault that names the step; a row of an earlier release with no hash gets the hash of this release on its first migrate, and the run notes it; (c) a check at generation: stego plan compares the body of each step of each released version with the digest that the release record holds, and refuses a change, so the fault is found before a release and not at a deploy; (d) both (b) and (c). A step that runs again when its body changes (runOnChange, the repeatable migrations of Flyway) is refused, because a DDL step is not idempotent. Recommendation: (d). (c) stops the fault where STEGO makes it, as STEGO writes every step and no person edits one; (b) is the second proof at the database, against a release built from another tree. STEGO writes each body from the declaration alone, so the false mismatches of a hand-written file (line endings, encoding) do not occur, and no repair command is given: the only fix is a new step. The within CHECK of postgres-adapter 6.10 then needs its own new step for a database that applied the step before 6.10. This changes the ledger table, CheckLedger and stego plan (builder of postgres-adapter and of Generating). Decision: (d), by the orchestrator under the Product owner's delegation, 2026-11-18. Part (b) holds in part already: the ledger records the SHA-256 digest of the body of each migration, and the ledger check of the migration job refuses a row whose digest differs (ST-SUP-RC01-OC11, proved by ST-SUP-RC01-OC11-T04). Thus a database that applied the step before postgres-adapter 6.10 is refused at the ledger check of the job, with a fault that does not name the step; the start check of the service runtime compares names only (ST-SUP-RP14-LC07). The build adds: the refusal names the migration and the remedy, and nothing repairs a digest (ST-SUP-RC01-OC51); the start check compares the digest of each migration of the release (ST-SUP-RP14-LC13); and the check against the base, which stego plan, stego apply and stego compat run, refuses a changed body of a migration that the record at the base lists (ST-GEN-INV38). The within CHECK of postgres-adapter 6.10 needs its own new step for a database that applied the within step before 6.10 (followups.md, sec-417 L2).

title: Must the problems of commands and of the tenant check have the type URI and the member case of the CRUD problems?
description: Found by walkthrough 5 (U3) and walkthrough 6 (U2), and open in walkthroughs 7, 8 and 9. A CRUD problem has a type under the declared error_type_base and snake_case members. A problem of a command, and the refusal tenant.not_provisioned of the tenant check, have the type about:blank or a bare word (such as idempotency-key-missing), camelCase members (such as ticketId), and for an unknown tenant the bare base as the type. Thus a client of one service needs two parsers for its problems. Prior art: RFC 9457 says that type is a URI reference that names the problem type, that about:blank means only the HTTP status, and that a client uses type, not detail, to tell problems apart; a bare word is a relative reference, which a client resolves against the request URL. AIP-193 gives one error model for each API (google.rpc.Status with ErrorInfo reason and domain). The Zalando REST guidelines ask for one problem form and snake_case members in every API. Options: (a) one form: each problem of the service, from CRUD, a command, a query, the tenant check and the idempotency check, has a type under error_type_base with a fixed path for each code, and snake_case members; the code stays the same, so a client that reads the code does not change; (b) keep each form and document both; (c) about:blank with a code member for each problem. Recommendation: (a). It needs a change of the command and query runtime (registry/runtime, which the runtime builder holds now), the tenancy component, and the problem forms in the OpenAPI document, in one new archetype version, because a client that reads the type sees a change. Decision: (a), Product owner, 2026-11-18: one problem form for each problem of a service; the type is under error_type_base with a fixed path for each code, the members are snake_case, and the codes stay the same; built in runtime v0.134.0 and one new archetype version, with a release note (ST-SUP-RC32-OC19, ST-SUP-RC33-OC12, ST-SUP-RC27-OC17).

title: How does an operator list the tenants of a service?
description: Found by walkthrough 6 (U10), and open in walkthroughs 7, 8 and 9. GET /stego/tenants answers 403 tenant.not_provisioned to the operator, because the operator's token names no provisioned tenant, and the service has no route that lists its tenants. The operator who provisions and retires tenants (ST-SUP-RC27-OC09) can thus not see which tenants exist, which are retired, or when each was provisioned, except by SQL on the tenant list. Prior art: Kubernetes lists namespaces through the API with a cluster-scope permission; the AWS Organizations ListAccounts call and the Azure management API list the tenants of an organization for its management role only; the Keycloak admin API lists realms for a realm admin of the master realm. Options: (a) a route GET <base path>/stego/tenants, decided on a permission list_tenants of the service-level resource of the provisioning (as provision and retire are), outside the tenant check as the two provisioning routes are (ST-SUP-RC27-OC11), that pages the tenant list (ID, state, the times of provision and retire) with a cursor, and is audited; (b) a CLI or SQL view for the operator only, with no route; (c) no list: the operator keeps the list in the system that provisions. Recommendation: (a), because the operator already acts on the same resource for provision and retire, and a paged and audited route keeps the operator out of the database. It needs an output contract on the tenancy component and a permission in the provisioning settings. Decision: (a), Product owner, 2026-11-18: GET <base path>/stego/tenants, decided on the permission list_tenants of the resource of the provisioning, outside the tenant check as Provision and Retire are, paged with a cursor and audited (ST-SUP-RC27-OC16).

title: How does an operator rotate the password of a database login of a service with no window of failed connections?
description: Found by the eleventh walkthrough (W11-B6, steps 54, 59 and 60), 2026-11-18. PostgreSQL holds one password for each login, and a process of the service reads its connection string once, at start. Thus the documented method (docs/operations.md, Rotate a database password) is change, then roll: a request that needs a new connection between the ALTER ROLE and the end of the restart of both Deployments fails with 28P01; pooled connections stay open. The method of two logins does not work today: the migration job refuses a member of a role of the service that it did not grant (the role check of the tenancy migration). Options: (a) alternating logins: the runtime role becomes a NOLOGIN group, and the migration job grants it to two named logins, <service>_runtime_a and <service>_runtime_b; a rotation sets the password of the idle login, points the Secret to it and rolls, and the other login stays valid. This is the alternating-users strategy of AWS Secrets Manager. It changes the role check, the grants and each place that names the runtime login. (b) two passwords in the secret: the runtime reads the file of the connection string again at each new connection, and the file may hold two connection strings, the new one first; a connection tries the first and, on 28P01 only, the second. A rotation writes both into the Secret, waits until the kubelet writes the file, runs ALTER ROLE, and then removes the old one; no pod restarts. It needs the Component secret-files, which mounts the Secret as a file that Kubernetes updates in place. (c) No change: keep change, then roll, and its documented window. Recommendation: (b). It adds no role and no grant, it keeps the role checks, it works with the External Secrets Operator and Sealed Secrets, and it removes the restart. Prior art: AWS Secrets Manager rotation (single user with a short window, or alternating users), MySQL 8 dual passwords (RETAIN CURRENT PASSWORD), Vault dynamic database credentials (a new login for each lease), and the Kafka method of two SCRAM users that docs/operations.md gives, which works today because a Kafka ACL names any user.

title: After a restore of a service database to a time T0, how does STEGO reconcile SpiceDB and the consumers with the database?
description: Found by the eleventh walkthrough (W11-B4, step 61), 2026-11-18. docs/operations.md (Restore from a backup) gives the restore of the database with its owner and grants (pg_restore --create), the migration job after it, and the reset of each consumer group to one minute before T0. Three gaps have no tool: (0) a message of the destination authz that was pending at T0 goes to SpiceDB again after the restore, and its write (OPERATION_TOUCH) has no precondition, so a grant that the relay wrote after T0 and that a person removed after T0 comes back (security review of PR #435, H1); docs/operations.md gives a manual review today: list the pending authz messages before the start, start the worker Deployment alone, then delete each such relationship again with zed before the API starts. (1) SpiceDB keeps the tuples of the rows that the service made after T0, such as the 3 tuples of a technician that the restored database no longer holds; the row IDs are new UUIDs, so the tuples give access to nothing, but they stay for ever and a retire does not remove them. (2) The consumers of the service's events applied the events of the writes after T0, which the source no longer holds. Options for (0): a restore mode that lists the pending authz messages of a restored database and lets the operator discard each one before the start, with an audit row; or a precondition on each write (a SpiceDB precondition that the relationship is absent, or a revision of the message) so that an older write does not undo a newer delete. Options for (1) and (2): (a) a periodic job of the controller mode that, for each resource type of the declaration and each tenant, reads the tuples from SpiceDB in pages and stages, through the authz outbox, the delete of each tuple whose row the database does not hold, with an audit row; it also removes the tuples that a retire leaves (W11-B11). (b) a one-time mode of the binary, restore-check, which the operator runs after a restore with the time T0: it reports the orphan tuples and the events of the service's topic after T0 whose row the database does not hold, and with --apply deletes the orphan tuples; the consumers get the list of events. (c) No tool: the documented manual steps with zed relationship read and delete, and a read of the topic from T0. Recommendation: for (0), the restore mode that lists and discards, in the restore-check mode of (b); for (1) and (2), (b) first, because a restore is rare and the operator must see the list before a delete; then (a) for the tuples of a retire. Prior art: a Kubernetes controller reconciles from the source of truth and is level-triggered; the SpiceDB guidance for a dual write is a reconcile from the database of record; Stripe and payment systems run a reconciliation report against the ledger after an incident.

title: How does the idempotency store keep the answers that it replays, which can hold pii?
description: Found by walkthrough 12 (W12-B7, step 38), 2026-11-18. The idempotency store (ST-SUP-RP07) keeps the status, the headers and the body of each completed answer in clear in idempotency_keys.response_body for the retention of the key, 24 hours by default (ST-SUP-RP07-LC07), so it can replay the same answer to a retry with the same key and body (ST-SUP-RP07-LC03). An answer holds the fields of the row, also a pii field: the walkthrough found the email of a member in 4 stored answers. The audit and the events redact pii (ST-DECL-UC05-R06); the store does not. Prior art: Stripe (API v1) saves the status code and the body of the first request with a key, also a 500, replays it, compares the parameters of a retry, and prunes a key after at least 24 hours; it tells clients not to put pii in the key, and says nothing of pii in the stored body. The IETF draft draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-08 (October 2026) leaves what the server stores to the server ('idempotent cache'), asks it to publish its expiry policy, gives 400, 409 and 422 for a missing key, a request in progress and a changed payload, and has no privacy text on stored answers; its security text asks for a lookup key composed with attributes of the client, which ST-SUP-RP07-LC01 does (tenant and principal). Options: (a) redact each pii field in the stored answer and keep a hash of the full answer for the replay check; a replay then gives the redacted body, or reads the row again, which is not the first answer; (b) seal the stored answer with the key ring of ST-DECL-Q44 (AES-256-GCM, the place tenant, principal and key as associated data), so the replay is exact and a dump of the table holds no pii in clear; it needs the key ring in each service with an idempotency store, and a lost ring loses only the replays; (c) shorten the retention of a key whose answer holds a pii field, such as to 1 hour, which makes the exposure shorter but not zero; (d) keep it and document that the store holds the answers in clear for the retention, as a database at rest. Recommendation: (b), with (d) until it is built, because it keeps the exact replay that ST-SUP-RP07-LC03 needs, reuses the key ring of ST-DECL-Q44, and does not change the contract of a client. Decision: (b), with (d) until (b) is built. The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: the stored answer is sealed with the key ring of ST-DECL-Q44, which keeps the exact replay of ST-SUP-RP07-LC03; until it is built, the docs state that the store keeps each answer for 24 h. Built (runtime v0.138.0, ST-SUP-RP07-LC13): a service with a secret or a pii field reads the key ring and seals each stored answer, with the prefix s1: on its fingerprint. A service with no secret and no pii field keeps its answers in clear for the retention, as (d) states: such an answer holds no personal data, and a key ring that no operator needs would add a Secret to each service. The orchestrator decided this scope on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation.

title: How do the people of a tenant get to read the rows that a worker makes with no parent?
description: Found by walkthrough 13 (W13-B4, D12, steps 18 and 19), 2026-11-18. A worker that creates a row with no parent, such as a ledger entry or a daily total, relates the row only to the tenant resource tenant:<base64url tenant>/<base64url tenant> (ST-SUP-Q164 (b), ST-SUP-RP10-LC17). A person can read such a row only through a relation of the type tenant, such as permission view = tenant->auditor. No route and no declaration writes a relation of a person on the tenant resource: Provision writes its admins on the service-level resource <resource type>:<base64url tenant>/<base64url service> (ST-SUP-RC27-OC09), which the row does not reach, and a command can write only relations of the entities that it writes. The walkthrough wrote the grant with zed, which no doc showed; docs/fills.md now shows it. Prior art: Zanzibar and SpiceDB model a hierarchy with a parent relation and an arrow (folder->viewer on a document); Google Cloud IAM lets a grant on an organization or a folder reach each project under it. Options: (a) Provision also writes the tuple tenant:<q>#service@<resource type>:<q> that relates the tenant resource to the service-level resource of the same tenant, and Retire deletes it; the schema then decides who reads, such as permission auditor_view = service->admin on the type tenant and view = tenant->auditor_view on the row; one tuple for each tenant, no new route, and the admins of Provision reach the rows; (b) Provision takes a second list of people and writes a declared relation of the type tenant for each, as it writes admins; (c) the declaration gives a worker a parent row that a command on the service-level resource creates, and the docs show the pattern; no runtime change, but each such service needs one more entity and command; (d) keep the grant by zed, and document it (today). Recommendation: (a), because it follows the parent pattern of Zanzibar, keeps each grant in the schema, and uses the admins that Provision already writes; (c) stays possible for a finer grant. Decision: (a). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: Provision relates the tenant resource to the service-level resource (tenant#service, the Zanzibar parent pattern), so the schema decides who reads the rows a worker makes with no parent.

title: How does a consumer of a change event get the state of the row, such as the amount of a transaction?
description: Found by walkthrough 13 (W13-B5, D04, D11, step 18), 2026-11-18. A change event holds only the entity, the action and the row ID, so no pii or secret value leaves the service (ST-SUP-RC20-OC40). subscriptions.md told the consumer to call the API of the source service, but a worker handle has no network client (ST-SUP-RC32-OC01), so the ledger of the walkthrough could not get the amount of a transaction. Prior art: Martin Fowler, 'What do you mean by Event-Driven?' (2017), names event-carried state transfer: the event holds the data that a consumer needs, so the consumer keeps its own copy and does not call the source, at the cost of duplicated data and eventual consistency; event notification, the form of STEGO today, needs a call back to the source. Debezium change events hold the whole row before and after the change (the envelope before, after, source, op, ts_ms), and its connectors leave out or mask columns with column.exclude.list and column.mask.with or column.mask.hash. CloudEvents puts the payload in data and names its schema in dataschema; its privacy text says that sensitive data should not be in the context attributes, and should be encrypted or left out of data. Options: (a) event-carried state: the event holds each declared field of the row, never a secret field, and a pii field only when the declaration chooses it; (b) a consumer query client: the worker handle gets a client of the queries of the source service, with a service identity, a timeout and a retry, which couples the consumer to the availability of the source; (c) a declared projection: the entity declares the fields that its change events carry, such as events: {fields: [wallet_id, kind, amount]}; validate refuses a secret field, a pii field needs a stated reason, the payload adds the member data with those fields, and stego compat holds the projection as it holds an API, so a field that a consumer reads is not removed without a major version. Recommendation: (c), which is event-carried state with an explicit contract: the source chooses each field that leaves the service, no secret can leave, the default stays the form of today, and the consumer needs no network client. (b) is not recommended: a worker that waits for another service breaks the isolation of a run and the order of the outbox. Decision: (c). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: a declared projection; a change event carries only the fields that the declaration lists, secret fields are refused, a pii field needs a stated reason, and stego compat holds the projection. Prior art: event-carried state transfer, Debezium column masking, CloudEvents data and dataschema.

title: How does a command count the wrong attempts of a compare-only secret, when a refusal commits nothing?
description: Found by the security review of PR #444 (M3), 2026-11-18, on the PIN example of docs/fills.md. A fill checks a compare-only secret with Compared.Matches and returns a declared refusal, such as pin.wrong, for a wrong value. Run commits only when the fill returns no error (ST-SUP-RP10-LC06, ST-SUP-RP10-LC07), so a counter of wrong attempts that the fill writes before the refusal rolls back with it, and the runtime has no limit of its own. A caller who may operate the wallet, such as with a stolen session, can try the 10,000 PINs of 4 digits in some minutes. Prior art: NIST SP 800-63B (5.2.2) asks a verifier to limit failed attempts on one account to at most 100 for a memorized secret; card schemes block a PIN after 3 wrong tries, with the count kept by the issuer across sessions; OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet asks for a lockout or a growing delay per account, not only per source address. Options: (a) a declared attempt counter: a field such as `attempts: {counts: pin, limit: 5}` on the entity, which Compared.Matches updates through the handle, and which a declared refusal commits in a short transaction of its own, after the rollback of the command, as the audit row of a failed command is written; at the limit the check refuses with a declared refusal until a command resets it; (b) a refusal that commits: a declared refusal may state `commit: [field]`, so the runtime commits the writes of those fields only; this is general, but each such refusal must prove that it writes nothing else; (c) no runtime change: the docs ask for a limit at the gateway or per caller and wallet (today). Recommendation: (a), because it keeps the rule that a refusal commits nothing of the business change, holds the count with the secret on the row, and follows the per-account limit of NIST and OWASP. Decision: (a). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: a declared attempt counter, committed in a short transaction of its own after the refusal rolls back the command (NIST SP 800-63B rate limiting, OWASP authentication guidance).

title: Does a worker get read-only access to an entity (reads), so that a list does not need write access and secrets?
description: Found by the security review of PR #444 (L2), 2026-11-18. A worker reads rows only through the repository of an entity in its writes (ST-SUP-RP10-LC02, ST-SUP-RP10-LC17), so a worker that only lists wallets, such as sum-balances in docs/fills.md, must declare writes: [Wallet]. It can then Reveal the readable secret api_key of each wallet of the tenant and update or delete each wallet. A fault or a compromised fill of a report leaks or changes each secret. A query already has reads with read-only access and no secret field (ST-SUP-RP11). Prior art: least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder, 1975); PostgreSQL GRANT SELECT apart from INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE; Kubernetes RBAC verbs get and list apart from update. Options: (a) a worker declares reads: [Entity] beside writes; the worker contract gives a read-only repository (Get and declared lists, no lock, no Create, Update or Delete) whose value type has no secret field, as the value of a query does, and SpiceDB decides the worker permission as for writes; (b) as (a), but the read value keeps a readable secret when the declaration states reads_secrets: true with a reason; (c) no change; the docs ask to put a secret in an entity of its own that a broad worker does not write (today). Recommendation: (a), because it gives a report worker the least access, reuses the read-only value of the query component, and keeps a secret out of each worker that does not need it. Decision: (a). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: a worker may declare reads, which gives a read-only repository whose values hold no secret field, as a query's values hold none.

title: How does the apply command of the generated CLI write to a service that requires an Idempotency-Key?
description: Found by the follow-up worker, run 17, 2026-11-18, when it proved the apply lookup of the CLI against a generated rest-crud service (ST-SUP-RC04-OC23-T06). A declaration can require the Idempotency-Key header on a create and a patch (idempotency required_on, ST-SUP-RC30-OC01); the service then answers 400 to a write with no key. The apply command of the CLI (ST-SUP-RC04) sends no key, because the HTTPS client that the CLI uses refuses the header: only the client of the API proxy sends it, as the other clients do not retry and so cannot keep its promise (ST-SUP-RC02-OC07). So apply cannot create or patch a resource of such a service, and the CLI reports the status failed. The proof gives each POST a key in a TLS front in front of the service. Prior art: the Stripe SDKs make a key for each write and send the same key again when they retry a write after a network error; the IETF draft draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header asks a client to send the same key when it retries. Options: (a) the CLI sends a new key on each apply write and does not retry, and ST-SUP-RC02-OC07 allows the header for the CLI too; (b) as (a), and the CLI retries an uncertain write once with the same key, so the status unknown occurs less often; ST-SUP-RC04-OC25 then says that a retry with the same key is not a repeated write; (c) no change to the CLI: generation refuses a service that has the cli-application component and requires a key on a create or a patch, or the README says that apply cannot write to it. Recommendation: (b), as the prior art does; (a) is the smallest change. Decision: (b). The orchestrator decided this on 2026-11-18 under the Product owner's delegation: the generated CLI sends a new Idempotency-Key on each write and retries once with the same key, so a retried write cannot run twice.

title: What happens to the copies of a value that a release wrote while its field was public, after the seal contract makes the field secret?
description: Found by walkthrough 14 (W14-B2, steps 33 and 46), 2026-11-18. A seal (decision ST-DECL-Q44) moves a field that the base stores in clear to its sealed column, and its contract step drops the clear column. But the releases before the seal wrote the value in clear in other places too: the audit rows of each create, update and pii read (public.audit_event, with before, after and patch), the entries of the audit sink (stego_audit_sink.entries), the outbox messages (stego_outbox.messages), the Kafka topics that the relay wrote, and each backup. After the contract of patient-insurance-seal the walkthrough found 228 insurance numbers in each of the three tables and 81 of 118 in a pg_dump; no row that a release after the expand step wrote holds one. The audit rows are hash-chained (ST-SUP-RP05), so a plain UPDATE of an old row breaks the chain check. Prior art: (1) Crypto-shredding: each value is encrypted with a key of its subject, and the deletion of the key erases each copy, also in backups (AWS and Confluent guidance on GDPR erasure in event logs); it does not help for copies that were written in clear before. (2) GDPR erasure in event-sourced systems: forgettable payloads (Mathias Verraes: the event holds a reference, and the value is in a store that can delete it), and copy-and-replace of a stream (Greg Young), which makes a new stream and loses the old hashes. (3) Redaction that keeps a hash chain valid: Amazon QLDB redacts a revision and keeps its digest, so the journal still verifies; Trillian and Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162) commit to the hash of each leaf, so the leaf data can go while the inclusion proofs stay valid; the CT redaction draft (draft-strad-trans-redaction) was not adopted, so a log never changes a leaf it published. (4) Debezium and the transactional outbox: the outbox row is deleted at once after its insert or after its delivery, because the log reader has it; Kafka removes a key with a tombstone and log compaction, but not the earlier records within the retention. (5) OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet and NIST SP 800-92: never write a secret to a log or an audit record; write a keyed hash (HMAC) when a reader must match it, because a plain hash of a short value such as an insurance number is found by brute force. Options: (a) the seal contract deletes, in its migration, the outbox messages that the relay delivered and the audit sink entries that the sink delivered, for the entity of the field, and the audit maintenance keeps no delivered entry after its window; undelivered rows stay, so no event is lost; (b) an audit row stores a keyed hash (HMAC with a key of the key ring) of each field of sensitivity pii, and the declaration can mark a public field as one that may become secret, so its audit value is a keyed hash too; this does not change rows that are there; (c) a documented redaction run, as the owner role, that replaces the value of the field in the old audit rows with a tombstone that holds the keyed hash of the value, with a new hash version whose row hash commits to a hash of each member, so the chain verifies after the redaction (as QLDB does); the rows before that hash version need a signed redaction record that names each row and its old hash; (d) document, in the seal steps, that each copy that a release wrote while the field was public stays: in the audit rows, the audit sink, the outbox, the topics of the consumers and each backup, until the retention of each ends, and that the operator must treat these as data of the old class. Recommendation: (d) now, which this change does, with (a) in the next release of the postgres adapter, because it is safe and cheap and removes two of the three tables; then (c) as its own design, because the audit chain is the evidence of ST-BO03 and a redaction must be verifiable; and (b) for pii fields only when a reader needs to match a value. A field that can become secret should be declared secret from its first release. Decision of the Product owner, 2026-11-18: (d) now, in the seal steps of docs/schema-changes.md; (a) next; (c) as its own later design; (b) only for pii fields where a reader must match a value.

title: Does a replica report ready when its database does not hold a table or a column of its schema manifest?
description: Found by walkthrough 15 (W15-B4, step 35), 2026-11-18. The contract step of a later release changed the database, and then a roll back started the replicas of an earlier release. The migration job of that release refused the database, which is correct. But each replica started, because the ledger holds the last migration of its release (ST-SUP-RP14-LC07), and a database that does not hold the manifest is an alert and not a refusal (decision on finding F10 of the schema-change research, owner, 2026-11-13; ST-SUP-RP14-LC06). The log said 'the database does not satisfy the schema manifest; the service starts', /readyz and /readyz/modes answered 200, and each write answered 500, because each statement names the column that the contract dropped (SQLSTATE 42703). Thus a rollout of the earlier release does not stop at its first replica, and Kubernetes removes the replicas that serve. PR #452 covers one case: a replica of the release of the expand step of a seal goes on after the contract, because it changes to the statements after the contract on SQLSTATE 42703 (ST-SUP-RP10-LC49 in #452). It does not cover: a release before the expand step of a seal, a drop, a rename or a retype, after the contract (42703); a release before the removal of an entity, after the contract (42P01); and a replica that starts on a database that a person changed by hand. Prior art: (1) Kubernetes keeps a replica that is not ready out of the endpoints of its Service, and a rolling update does not remove an old replica until a new one is ready (maxUnavailable, maxSurge, progressDeadlineSeconds); a failed liveness probe restarts the container, and the Kubernetes guidance is to fail readiness, not liveness, when the replica cannot use a dependency ('Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes'). (2) Flyway ignores by default the applied migrations that the application does not know (ignoreMigrationPatterns '*:future'), so a roll back starts, and it gives no check that the schema still holds what the older code reads. (3) The expand and contract pattern (Martin Fowler, 'ParallelChange'; Prisma and PlanetScale guidance) holds that a roll back is safe only to a release that runs on the contracted schema; a release before it must not take traffic. Options: (a) The start check puts each fault of a missing table and of a missing column of the manifest in a list of its own (manifest.Mismatch.Blocking), except a column that the manifest marks as one that a later contract may drop (manifest.Column.Droppable), which is the clear column of each seal whose last step in the declaration is expand, because that release goes on after the contract (#452). When the list is not empty, the replica starts, logs and alerts as now, and each of its modes answers not ready with the table or the column and the remedy, so a rollout stops at its first replica and the replicas of the release before go on serving. Each other fault still alerts and starts ready (F10). The replica stays not ready until it starts again, because the remedy is a roll forward. (b) The same faults refuse the start, as a missing migration does (ST-SUP-RP14-LC07), with a stage of their own: the rollout also stops, but the container restarts in a loop with back-off, and the alert repeats at each start. (c) Each fault makes the replica not ready, also a missing index, grant, trigger or policy, with which the code still runs: a drift that F10 decided to alert would then stop the service at the next restart of all replicas, such as a node drain. (d) Keep the behaviour and document that a roll back after a contract is not supported. Recommendation: (a), because it changes only the faults with which each statement on the table fails, it keeps F10 for each other fault, and it fits #452. The changes of (a): ST-SUP-RP14-LC06, ST-SUP-RP09-LC05 and ST-SUP-RC01-OC12 get one sentence each, and the new contract ST-SUP-RP15-LC05 states Blocking and Droppable.

title: In which order does a consuming worker apply a record that an offset reset sends again, when a later record of the same row is parked?
description: Found by walkthrough 15 (W15-B2, steps 11 to 15), 2026-11-18. Tenant alpha was provisioned in the source before the consumer billing, on purpose. Billing refused the created events of alpha with unknown-tenant (ST-SUP-RP01-LC36). Then alpha was provisioned in billing, and an update of a shipment of alpha reached billing: its fill found no invoice, failed five times and was parked as poison (ST-SUP-RC35-OC06). The documented remedy (subscriptions.md, 'Order of provision and start') is an offset reset to the earliest offset. The created event of the shipment then came again, but the inbox wrote it as a new message at the end of the queue, after the parked update of the same key (tenant, destination, resource key). The queue orders a key by its own sequence (ST-SUP-RP01-LC03), and a parked message holds back each later message of its key (ST-SUP-RP01-LC12). Thus not_acted ran the update again before the created event, and it parked again. acted is refused for a subscription (ST-SUP-RP01-LC13), and only discarded freed the key, which lost the update. Prior art (notes of core32, b2-prior-art.txt): (1) Axon Framework, sequenced dead-letter queue: a failed event and each later event of its sequence (the aggregate) go to the dead-letter queue, and processAny runs a sequence in order. A replay appended the replayed events at the end of a blocked sequence, so the event that would unblock it waited behind the dead letter that needs it (OrderCreated behind a parked OrderApproved; AxonIQ issue 515, rated priority 1). The fix (AxonIQ pull request 643) gives each dead letter its position in the stream: during a replay an event before every dead letter of its sequence is handled, an event that is already a dead letter is skipped, and each other event takes its place by position. AxonIQ also clears the dead letters on a reset by default. (2) Kafka keeps the order of a key only within its partition, by offset; Confluent's redirect pattern sends each later event of a failed item to the retry path and frees the item when its head clears, and DevGeist lists the failures of such per-key locks in production (stuck keys; a lock freed too early after a replay). Uber's retry topics and Spring Kafka's retry topics give up the order of a key. (3) Debezium puts the events of a row in one partition by key, and an incremental snapshot can send a READ of a row after its UPDATE; the guidance is to compare the source position or version, not the order of arrival. (4) NServiceBus does not keep an order: a retry goes back to the queue, and a saga that any of its messages can start, or a retry after 'saga not found', applies a message that came too early. Options: (a) The inbox writes the partition and the offset of each record into its message, and the order within a key is the order of the offsets for messages of the same partition, else the order of the queue. A record that an offset reset sends again takes its place before the later messages of its key, as in its topic; a record whose message is in the queue is not written again (ST-SUP-RP01-LC35, as now). In the walkthrough, the created event runs at once, because the parked update comes after it; not_acted then applies the update. (b) When a message of the inbox is done, each parked message of the same key that comes after it in that order and that was parked as poison goes back to pending with its attempts reset, the resolution not_acted and an audit row of the consuming worker. So the update that waited for its created event runs again with no person. Alone, (b) does not help here, because the created event never gets done while the update holds it back. (c) not_acted puts the message at the end of its key: the created event runs first here, but a resolved message runs after the later updates of its row, so an older value overwrites a newer one. (d) Keep the order and document that before an offset reset each parked message of the subscription must be discarded, and the lost changes repaired by hand. Recommendation: (a) and (b) together, as Axon did after the same failure: (a) puts the replayed record where it was in the topic, and (b) frees the key with no person once the cause is applied. A key whose partition changes, such as after partitions are added to the topic, falls back to the order of the queue, which is the order of today; the docs must say this. The changes of (a) and (b): ST-SUP-RP01-LC03, ST-SUP-RP01-LC12 and ST-SUP-RP01-LC35 get one sentence each, and the new contract ST-SUP-RP01-LC39 states (b).

title: Does a wrong parent argument to the repository of an entity with its own resource type fail at compile time?
description: Found by walkthrough 15 (W15-B3, steps 16 and 19), 2026-11-18. Parcel is under Shipment and has its own resource type, so it is not a child entity. The fill of dispatch-shipment gave the loaded shipment as the parent to parcels.Update. The code compiled, stego test and go build passed, and each call answered 500 at run time with the log line 'an update of Parcel that keeps its references takes no parent'. The same mistake on accounts gave the same 500. The generated function <Entity>Repository gives *command.Repository[T] for each entity, whose methods all take parents as a variadic argument, because a child entity (an entity with no resource type of its own) needs the loaded parent on each locked read, update and delete. For an entity with its own resource type the runtime refuses each parent of GetForUpdate, GetForDelete and Delete, and takes a parent on Update only when the update moves a reference to the new referenced row (ST-SUP-RP10-LC05, ST-SUP-RP10-LC17). docs/fills.md defines 'child entity' only in the table of worker lists. Prior art: the Go guidance is to let the type system refuse a call that can never be right (Effective Go; the 'make illegal states unrepresentable' rule of typed APIs); sqlc and Ent generate one typed method set for each table; the Kubernetes typed clients give a namespaced and a cluster-scoped resource different method sets, so a namespace argument to a cluster-scoped resource does not compile. Options: (a) For each entity with its own resource type, the generated <Entity>Repository gives *<Entity>Repo, a generated type that embeds *command.Repository[T] and has GetForUpdate(ctx, id), GetForDelete(ctx, id), Update(ctx, from, value) and Delete(ctx, from) with no parent; when the entity has a reference to an entity with a resource type, also Move(ctx, from, value, parents ...command.Ref), an update that changes a reference and takes the loaded value of each new referenced row. Create, List, ListForUpdate and Get keep their forms. A child entity keeps *command.Repository[T]. A wrong parent then fails in go build and stego test with 'too many arguments'. A fill that passed nil as the parent, or that gave the parents of a move to Update, must change: the first drops nil, the second calls Move. (b) Only Update loses its parents, as in (a), with Move; GetForUpdate, GetForDelete and Delete keep the runtime refusal. (c) stego test runs a static check of each fill (go/analysis) and refuses a parent argument to GetForUpdate, GetForDelete and Delete of such an entity with the file and the line; a parent of Update stays a run-time refusal, because only the values tell whether the update moves a reference. (d) Keep the API and document the rule, with the definition of a child entity in fills.md. Recommendation: (a), because each wrong parent of the walkthrough fails before a release, the methods of a child entity do not change, and a move is a call of its own that says what it does. The changes of (a): the new output contract ST-SUP-RC32-OC26. docs/fills.md gets the definition of a child entity where Update is described, in each option.

title: Which mark makes a member of a command message a secret, so that the OpenAPI document, the generated CLI and the stored answers treat it as one?
description: Found by the security review of PR #454 (L2), 2026-11-19. The request and response messages of a command come from the proto files of the declaration. The OpenAPI document gives each member of them as its protobuf JSON form (ST-SUP-RC20-OC53), with no mark for a secret. Thus the generated CLI (ST-SUP-RC04-OC32) gives a flag to a secret request member, such as a PIN or an API token, because it leaves out only a member that the document marks writeOnly or x-sensitive; the flag puts the value in the shell history and the process list. And no CLI command is Sensitive: an answer that holds a secret, such as an API key that a command makes and gives one time, goes to standard output and not only to --output-file. Also, the runtime keys the idempotency fingerprints and seals the stored answers only for a service with a secret or a pii field (ST-SUP-RP14-LC12, ST-SUP-RP07-LC13): a command of a service with no such field stores the answer that holds the API key in clear for 24 hours, and a plain SHA-256 fingerprint of a body with a short PIN lets a reader of the table guess the PIN. Prior art: protobuf has the standard field option debug_redact (FieldOptions field 16, protobuf 22 and later) for a field that holds credentials; C++ (v30) and Java redact it in debug output, and Go code reads it with FieldOptions.GetDebugRedact (protoslog redacts it in slog). google.api.field_behavior INPUT_ONLY marks a member of requests only, not a secret; protoc-gen-openapiv2 (grpc-gateway) uses only REQUIRED and OUTPUT_ONLY (readOnly) and ignores INPUT_ONLY, because OpenAPI 2 has no writeOnly; the gnostic protoc-gen-openapi (OpenAPI 3) maps INPUT_ONLY to writeOnly. protoc-gen-openapiv2 field options have read_only and no write_only. buf (protovalidate) has no sensitive mark. OpenAPI 3 has writeOnly (not in responses) and the format password (a hint to mask the value). Options. (a) The standard option [debug_redact = true] on a member marks it a secret. It needs no import, because it is in google/protobuf/descriptor.proto, and other tools redact the same member in logs. The rest-api component gives a marked member x-sensitive true and the format password, and writeOnly true in a request body; the CLI gives it no flag and makes each command whose success answer holds a marked member Sensitive; and a service with a marked member keys its fingerprints and seals its stored answers, as a service with a secret field does. (b) google.api.field_behavior = INPUT_ONLY: the compiler of STEGO resolves only the standard imports, so each declaration needs the googleapis protos; it marks no response member; and it means 'not in responses', not 'secret'. (c) A STEGO option, such as (stego.v1.secret) = true, from a proto that STEGO ships: an exact meaning, but each declaration imports a STEGO proto, and other tools do not know it. (d) A list in the declaration, such as secret_members of each command: no proto change, but the list and the message can differ, and a renamed member loses its mark. Recommendation: (a), because it is the mark of protobuf itself for this case, it needs no new import or declaration key, and it covers request and response members. A pii mark for command members is not in this question. The changes of (a): the new output contracts ST-SUP-RC20-OC54 (rest-api 4.22.0) and ST-SUP-RC04-OC33 (cli-application 1.13.0), and changes of ST-SUP-RP14-LC12 and ST-SUP-RC32-OC21 (command 1.16.0). docs/commands-queries-workers.md gets the mark in the section of the request and response messages.

title: How does a generated CLI know, after a 5xx answer, that the service keeps the key of the write, when the CLI is of another release than the service?
description: Found by the security review of PR #449 (LOW-1), 2026-11-18.
